family.name: Series & Defender
family.verdict: The original farm-gate-to-Sahara tool: slow, leaky, drafty, and still the shape every other boxy 4x4 gets measured against.
intro: Land Rover started in 1948 as a stopgap: Rover's chief designer Maurice Wilks proposed a light agricultural and utility vehicle, and the first prototype was skinned in Birmabright aluminium alloy because steel was rationed and aluminium wasn't. It was launched at the Amsterdam Motor Show in April that year, and the Series I, II, IIA and III that followed ran until 1985.

In 1983 the One Ten arrived with coil springs and permanent four-wheel drive borrowed from the [[range-rover/classic|Range Rover Classic]], followed by the Ninety in 1984. In 1990 they became the Defender 90, 110 and 130, and the line kept going until 29 January 2016, a 67-year run counted back to the 1948 original. The [[land-rover/discovery-1|Discovery]] (1989) took the same Range Rover chassis in a family-friendly direction.

Americans mostly know the classic Defender through a short official window: 525 NAS Defender 110s for 1993 (500 US, 25 Canada), then the NAS Defender 90 through 1997, before the 25-year import rule opened the gray-market floodgates. The badge returned in 2020 as the unibody [[land-rover/defender-l663|L663 Defender]], while the [[grenadier/station-wagon|Ineos Grenadier]] picked up the ladder-frame torch.

page.title: Land Rover 90 / 110 / Defender
page.eyebrow: LAND ROVER · NINETY / ONE TEN / DEFENDER · 1983–2016
page.verdict: A Series Land Rover that finally got coil springs, then refused to change anything else for 33 years. Americans got a few thousand officially; everyone else got a legend.

paragraphs: The classic Defender is what happens when a company finds the right answer in 1948 and spends the next six decades only fixing the bits that hurt. Under the slab-sided aluminium skin sits a steel ladder frame, two beam axles and bolted-on panels. It is not quick, quiet or watertight. It is, however, the vehicle that taught several generations of overlanders that you can rebuild anything in a campsite if the thing was designed by people who expected you to.

story.heading: FROM SERIES TO ONE TEN
paragraphs: By the early 1980s the leaf-sprung [[land-rover/series|Series III]] was feeling its age. Land Rover's fix was to raid its own luxury shelf: the One Ten of 1983 got coil springs front and rear and permanent four-wheel drive with a centre differential, both lifted from the [[range-rover/classic|Range Rover Classic]]. The short-wheelbase Ninety followed in 1984 and the long One Two Seven in 1985.

Engines were a grab bag at first: 2.25-litre petrol and diesel carry-overs, a 2.5 diesel making a heroic 68 hp from 1984, and the Rover 3.5 V8 that turned the 90 into something approaching brisk. A Diesel Turbo arrived in 1986, and in 1990 the 200Tdi finally gave the truck a diesel worth having, with 107 hp and 195 lb-ft. It is still the engine many gray-market shoppers go looking for, because there is very little on it that a laptop needs to diagnose.

story.heading: THE DEFENDER NAME, AND AMERICA
paragraphs: When the [[land-rover/discovery-1|Discovery]] arrived in 1989, the plain-named Land Rover needed a name of its own. It became the Defender 90, 110 and 130, with badges changing for the 1991 model year. The 300Tdi replaced the 200Tdi in 1994, the five-cylinder Td5 came in 1998, and the Ford-sourced 2.4 'Puma' diesel with a six-speed arrived in 2007. Through all of it, the basic shape barely moved.

North America's official ration started with the 1993 NAS (North American Specification) Defender 110: 525 trucks, 500 for the US and 25 for Canada, all Alpine White, all 3.9-litre V8 with a five-speed manual, full external roll cage and a numbered badge. The NAS Defender 90 followed from 1994, first as a soft-top and later with a removable fibreglass roof panel or a full hard-top, and the last 1997 trucks got a 4.0 V8 and a ZF four-speed automatic. ECD puts total NAS production at about 7,059.

story.heading: WHAT MADE IT SPECIAL
paragraphs: The genius is that almost nothing is precious. Body panels are aluminium bolted to a steel frame, the axles are solid, the transfer box is a two-speed LT230 with a centre diff you lock by hand when the going gets slippery, and the parts catalogue is still enormous decades later. Owners fix their own swivels, timing belts and outriggers because the job is genuinely within reach, and an aftermarket from Solihull to Vermont exists to help.

It also leaks, rattles, rusts at the steel bits and steers like a boat with opinions. That's the deal. In return you get short overhangs, a body you can see the corners of, a cabin you can hose out, and a silhouette so recognizable that Ineos built a whole company, and the [[grenadier/station-wagon|Grenadier]], around missing it. Love it or hate it, nobody has ever mistaken one for a crossover.

story.heading: HOW IT ENDED, AND THE 25-YEAR AFTERLIFE
paragraphs: US sales stopped after the 1997 model year; regulations arriving for 1998, including airbag and side-impact door requirements, made the old body uneconomic to certify. Production for everyone else ended on 29 January 2016, after a 67-year run counting the Series, and the name came back in 2020 on the unibody, independently sprung [[land-rover/defender-l663|L663 Defender]]. Whatever you think of the new one, it ended the era of the separate chassis and beam axles at Land Rover.

Meanwhile federal law did the rest. NHTSA lets a vehicle at least 25 years old, counted from its date of manufacture, be imported without meeting FMVSS, so every year another batch of Euro-market 90s and 110s becomes legal. That market has teeth: in 2014 Homeland Security agents seized more than two dozen Defenders imported by one North Carolina enthusiast over suspected VIN swaps; after a legal fight they were found correctly imported and ordered returned in 2015. Not every owner was so lucky: Hagerty reported one whose undocumented truck was seized and apparently lost. Buy the paperwork before you buy the truck.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · NAS DEFENDERS
callout.title: The 7,000-ish Defenders America got officially
paragraphs: 1993 NAS 110: 525 built over about a year in a special area at Solihull, 500 for the US and 25 for Canada, all Alpine White, with 3.9 V8, five-speed manual, full external cage, basket roof rack, deep-dish wheels and a sequence-numbered NAS badge. Clean ones now trade near $200,000, according to Atlantic British.

1994–1997 NAS 90: soft-tops first, then a removable fibreglass roof panel and a full hard-top; ECD says cracking fibreglass tops were an early problem. Colours across the run included Coniston Green, Portofino Red, Arles Blue, Beluga Black, Alpine White and AA Yellow. The 1997 run added a 4.0-litre V8 and ZF four-speed automatic, and the run closed with the 300-unit Limited Edition D90 station wagon in Willow Green with a white roof.

page.engineering_intro: The 90/110 is a Series Land Rover rebuilt on Range Rover hardware: a boxed steel ladder frame carrying beam axles on coil springs, permanent four-wheel drive through a two-speed transfer box with a lockable centre differential, and aluminium body panels bolted to a steel bulkhead. That layout makes it tough and endlessly repairable, and also explains its two big weaknesses: steel parts rust where mud and water sit, and the drivetrain was built for a 1980s power level.

engineering.note: Mild steel; rear crossmember and outriggers rot first.
Panels oxidise and lift paint rather than rusting; the steel bulkhead and footwells do rust.
Front and rear coils, lifted from the 1970 Range Rover.
Lock it before prolonged wheelspin; the stock diff's small gears can fail.
Used through the Defender run (early V8 One Tens had the LT95), plus Discovery 1 and Range Rover Classic.
Chrome balls and seals need periodic attention; preload set with shims.

buying_checks.head: Paperwork and VIN first
buying_checks.body: Match the VIN plate on the brake servo with the number stamped on the front chassis rail. For gray-market imports, make sure the build date really is 25+ years old; federal agents have seized Defenders over alleged VIN swaps, and owners without paperwork lost them.

buying_checks.head: Rear crossmember
buying_checks.body: It takes towing and winching loads and rots from the inside out. Fibreglass, fresh underseal or chunky checker plate can hide it, so get under with a light and ask for the underside to be cleaned.

buying_checks.head: Bulkhead, footwells and outriggers
buying_checks.body: Check the bulkhead sides, bottom corners and the top under the vent flaps, plus the footwells and the outrigger behind the front wheel. Repair is real money; a new bulkhead runs about £1,600 in the UK.

buying_checks.head: Swivel balls and steering play
buying_checks.body: Pitted chrome balls chew their seals and wear the swivel pins. Vague or wobbly steering with excess play points here; budget for rebuild kits if the balls are rusty or weeping.

buying_checks.head: Transfer box noise and leaks
buying_checks.body: Listen for whine and clunks in low range. Oil leaking from the LT230 can coat the transmission handbrake shoes; check the rear output seal and intermediate shaft area.

buying_checks.head: 300Tdi timing belt history
buying_checks.body: Ask whether the revised timing kit (Land Rover STC4096L-type, with flanged crank pulley and spaced idler) has been fitted. Early setups could let the belt track off and wear.

buying_checks.head: Td5 oil in the loom
buying_checks.body: Pull the barrel connector between the engine and injector harnesses. Oil there means it's wicking toward the ECU under the seat.

buying_checks.head: NAS authenticity
buying_checks.body: A real 1993 NAS 110 or 1994–97 NAS 90 carries a numbered NAS badge and a US-market VIN. Plenty of Euro trucks have been dressed up as NAS; check against the registry discussions on Defender Source.

repairs.title: Swivel housing rebuild and preload
repairs.time: ≈ 1 hour both sides for a shim/preload adjustment; longer for a full rebuild
repairs.symptoms: Grease or oil weeping from the swivel seal, pitted chrome ball, wobbly or vague steering.
repairs.fix: Support the chassis on stands, pull the wheels and disconnect the track rod. Rebuild with new bearings, seals and gaskets, fit the swivel pins with shims, torque lower then upper bolts, and check turning effort with a spring balance at the track-rod bore before fitting the seal. Workshop-manual text quoted on Defender2: 1.16–1.46 kg once initial inertia is overcome, with the swivel bearing housing-to-axle bolts at 73 Nm, lower swivel pin bolts at 25 Nm and top pin bolts at 65 Nm (thread sealant STC50552 on the pin bolts). The manuals disagree, though: a RAVE table quoted on AULRO matches those bolt torques (65 Nm upper, 25 Nm lower, 73 Nm housing-to-axle), but a 05/99 workshop-manual table quoted in the same thread gives 78 Nm for both upper and lower pins, and a Defender2 owner reports the older manual's 22–28 Nm lower figure against 78 Nm in a newer one. The 1983–1995 workshop manual and Haynes give a turning effort of 3.6–4.5 kg rather than 1.16–1.46 kg. Use the manual for your exact axle [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. Add or remove top-pin shims to adjust, then refill with one-shot grease.
repairs.tools: Axle stands, spring balance, vernier, torque wrench · Rovers North RNA3178 swivel rebuild kit with ball (1994–98 Defender, one side) · one-shot grease

parts.name: Britpart DA3167P swivel housing repair kit (bearings, seals, shims; no ball)
Front axle swivel ball oil seal LR059968
One-shot swivel housing grease STC3435 (2 sachets)

repairs.title: Top up a leaking swivel with one-shot grease
repairs.symptoms: Grease smeared on the inside of the wheel and around the swivel seal retainer.
repairs.fix: Remove the seal retaining ring (six 8 mm nuts on the Defender), clean the seal area, then turn the wheel to full lock away from the side you're filling so the housing doesn't overlap the ball, and fill through the filler plug. One pack per side is roughly right; the grease is runny.
repairs.tools: 8 mm socket, rags · one-shot swivel grease (Britpart and Land Rover packs)

parts.name: Front axle swivel ball oil seal LR059968

repairs.title: 300Tdi timing belt with revised kit
repairs.symptoms: Due on the service interval, belt edge wear, or debris inside the timing cover; early-type kits can let the belt track off.
repairs.fix: Lock the cam and crank with the timing tool, remove the front cover, fit the revised kit (flanged crank pulley, idler with integral spacer, tensioner, gasket). On early-type engines, remove the separate spacer washer because the new idler includes it. Land Rover later reduced the torque used to tension the belt (applied to the tensioner before its bolt is tightened) to 11 Nm, according to both Glencoyne and an AULRO member, and earlier manuals may not include the change: Glencoyne gives the old figure as 15 Nm, the AULRO member as 14 Nm. This is the belt-tension setting, not the bolt's clamping torque.
repairs.tools: Timing tool DA3140, torque wrench · STC4096L modified timing belt kit

parts.name: 300Tdi timing belt kit and front cover gasket

repairs.title: Td5 injector harness oil leak
repairs.time: Short for the injector harness; much bigger if the main loom is contaminated
repairs.symptoms: Oil and dust on the ECU plug under the driver's seat, misfires or running issues.
repairs.fix: The injector harness lives inside the rocker cover; oil wicks out through the plug seal and along the main loom to the ECU. Remove the acoustic cover, unplug the barrel connector and check for oil. Replace the injector harness; if oil has reached the main engine loom, replace that too. Light contamination can be flushed with contact cleaner, but replacement is the real fix.
repairs.tools: Basic hand tools, contact cleaner · genuine injector harness

parts.name: Td5 injector harness and rocker cover gasket

repairs.title: LT230 rear output seal and flange
repairs.symptoms: Oil running down the back of the transfer box, contaminated transmission handbrake.
repairs.fix: Confirm the source first: on an LT230 the intermediate shaft is a common leak. Drop the propshaft, remove the rear flange nut and flange (can be done in situ), tap off the dust cap, replace the rear seal and felt washer, then refit with a new M20 nyloc nut and fresh flange bolts torqued to spec.
repairs.tools: Large socket for M20 nut, flange holding tool, seal driver · rear output seal, felt washer, nyloc nut

parts.name: LT230 output flange oil seal FRC7043
FTC4939SET transfer box output seal kit (2 pcs)
LT230 output flange, nut and dust shield

repairs.title: Chassis outrigger and rear crossmember repair
repairs.cost: Outriggers about £30 each; a galvanised replacement chassis supplied and fitted for under £5,000 (UK), per PistonHeads
repairs.symptoms: Perforated outriggers, flaking rear crossmember, failed inspection.
repairs.fix: Cut out rotten outriggers or crossmember sections and weld in new ones, then treat the inside of the frame. If the rot is widespread, a galvanised chassis swap is often the better answer.
repairs.tools: Welder, grinder, cavity wax · replacement outriggers and crossmember

parts.name: STC8651 rear crossmember with extensions (Defender 110 to VIN WA159806)

repairs.title: Bulkhead footwell repair
repairs.cost: Repair panels cheap; used bulkhead from about £650, new about £1,600 (UK)
repairs.symptoms: Damp carpets, holes in the footwells or the bottom corners of the bulkhead.
repairs.fix: Strip interior trim, cut back to clean steel, weld in repair panels, then seal and wax. Fix the leak source too (windscreen and vent seals) or it will happen again.
repairs.tools: Welder, grinder, seam sealer · footwell repair panels

parts.name: Footwell repair panels (search; confirm Defender fitment)

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: 235/85R16 is the classic factory size on 110s and the 'sweet spot' most owners recommend; NAS D90s came on 265/75R16. 255/85R16 (about 33") is the popular upgrade and generally fits at stock height, but owners report rubbing on the front radius arms at full lock (fix by winding out the steering stops), against the 45 L auxiliary tank on 110s, and close to the spring brackets at full compression on 90s.

faq.q: Can I import a Defender into the US?
faq.a: Yes, if it's at least 25 years old counted from its date of manufacture: NHTSA lets those vehicles in without meeting FMVSS (declared under Box 1 on the HS-7). Newer trucks must comply, which a classic Defender can't. Check EPA and your state's emissions rules too, and make sure the VIN, chassis number and build date line up.

Everything built at least 25 years before the import date, so in late 2026 that's trucks built up to late 2001. That covers 200Tdi, 300Tdi, V8 and early Td5 Defenders (the Td5 arrived in 1998). The Ford 'Puma' Defenders from 2007 won't start qualifying until 2032.

North American Specification Defenders were the ones Land Rover sold new in the US and Canada: 525 1993 Defender 110s (500 US, 25 Canada) and Defender 90s from 1994 to 1997, all V8. About 7,059 were built in total.

faq.q: Why did Land Rover stop selling the Defender in the US after 1997?
faq.a: Regulations taking effect for 1998, including airbag and side-impact door requirements, made it too expensive to keep the old body compliant. The Defender name returned to US showrooms in 2020 on the all-new L663.

For a gray-market truck, the 300Tdi is the simple, mechanical favourite; check the revised timing kit has been fitted. The 200Tdi is cruder but similar. The Td5 is more powerful (122 hp) but electronically managed, so check for oil in the injector loom. In the US, NAS trucks are all 3.9/4.0 V8, which is thirsty but easy to service.

faq.q: Which years are the best to buy?
faq.a: For a 25-year-legal import, the Tdi years. ECD rates the 300Tdi (1994–98) the top choice for longevity and the 200Tdi (1990–94) a close second, and Classic Car Hub says if you remember one engine number, make it 300Tdi. Early '10P' Td5s have known head and oil-pump-drive problems, so look for a 15P engine or proof of repair. Among the Puma trucks, PistonHeads points to a 2011. Whatever the engine, the chassis, bulkhead and rear crossmember decide what it's worth.
faq.src: ECD · CLASSIC CAR HUB · HERITAGE PARTS CENTRE · PISTONHEADS

faq.q: What fuel economy should I expect?
faq.a: ECD estimates 12–16 mpg for the factory V8 (12–14 in real-world use), 23–27 mpg for the 300Tdi, 22–26 mpg for the Td5 and 20–25 mpg for the Puma diesels; it doesn't say how they were measured. Roof racks, big tyres and a heavy right foot will take you well under those.

faq.q: How much can a classic Defender tow?
faq.a: CarsGuide lists 3,500 kg (7,716 lb) braked for 2004 Defender 90, 110 and 130 variants, and GoAuto gives the same 3,500 kg braked / 750 kg unbraked for the 2009 Defender 90. Unbraked trailers are limited to 750 kg. Check your own truck's plate and handbook; the rear crossmember condition matters more than the brochure number.

faq.q: When do I lock the centre diff?
faq.a: Whenever you expect prolonged wheelspin: mud, snow, ice, sand, steep loose climbs. The LT230's stock centre diff has small gears that can fail if a front wheel spins for long, and the diff lock removes that risk. Unlock it on grippy surfaces to avoid driveline wind-up.

The aluminium panels don't rust, but they oxidise, lifting paint and eventually perforating. The steel parts rust: chassis rear crossmember, outriggers, bulkhead footwells and corners, door frames and hinge mounts. Budget for welding unless the truck already has a galvanised chassis.

mods.why: Stock springs sag with age and accessories. Heavier springs and better shocks restore ride height and add an inch or two for 255/85 tyres.
Open diffs front and rear; an air locker or ATB limited-slip transforms progress on articulated ground.

mods.why: Rebuilt or brand-new LT230s, taller ratios for big tyres, ATB centre diffs and heavy-duty 300M shafts.
Seals, swivel kits, panels, NAS-specific trim, timing kits: these are the US and UK catalogues the community actually uses.
When the frame is past welding, a hot-dip galvanised replacement chassis is the permanent fix.

baseline_service.intro: Assume nothing has been done. Most of these trucks are 25 to 40 years old and have usually had several owners. Change every fluid, re-grease the swivels and propshafts, and confirm the timing-belt history on a Tdi. Specs differ between the US V8 (NAS) trucks and the 200/300Tdi, Td5 and Puma diesels, so identify the engine and gearbox first. Fill the axles, transfer box and swivels to their level plugs on level ground rather than trusting a book capacity.

items.spec: NAS 3.9 V8: API SG/SH, SAE 5W-30 or 5W-40 · ≈6.7 L with filter. 300Tdi: ≈6.65 L with filter (Comma lists 10W-40). Td5: 7.8 L with filter, 5W-40 or 5W-50 (Haynes). 2.4 Puma (2007–12 MY) and 2.2 (2012 MY on): 6.85 L service fill with filter, 5W-30 to WSS-M2C913-B or C, or WSS-M2C934-B for the 2.2 with DPF (Land Rover oil chart)
items.interval: At purchase, then every 5,000–6,000 mi (Comma: 10,000 km / 6 months for the 300Tdi)
items.note: The V8 and Tdi engines use the short spin-on filter. The Td5 also has a centrifugal oil-filter rotor that needs servicing.

items.interval: At purchase; more often in dust
items.note: Check that the dump valve at the bottom of the airbox isn't split, because it lets unfiltered air in.

items.spec: Revised kit (flanged crank pulley, idler, tensioner). V8 and Td5 use timing chains, not belts
items.interval: Every 60,000 mi or 5 years per Lucky8. Glencoyne says 60k or 72k depending on model. Do it at purchase if there's no record
items.note: Land Rover revised the 300Tdi tensioner, idler and bottom pulley because belts were wearing early. A yellow paint square on the timing cover was meant to show the fix had been done, but it isn't reliable.

items.spec: 50/50 ethylene glycol antifreeze and water · NAS V8 ≈12.8 L. 300Tdi ≈11.1 L
items.interval: At purchase, then every 2 years (Comma: 40,000 km / 24 months)
items.note: The aluminium V8 can't take overheating. Check the radiator for blocked fins and the viscous fan for drag while the system is drained.

parts.name: ETC4765 thermostat (V8 Defender / Discovery / Range Rover)

items.spec: Handbook: ATF M2C33-F or G (as quoted on AULRO) · ≈2.4 L (Comma lists its 75W-80 MTF for the 300Tdi R380)
items.note: Check the level at the side filler with the truck level. A notchy second gear or third-gear synchro problem on an R380 isn't fixed by changing the oil. A 1993 NAS 110 (LT77) data set lists 2.67 L.

parts.name: R380 gearbox oil and drain/fill plugs

items.spec: Dexron IID ATF · 9.1 L listed total fill
items.note: Draining the pan only replaces part of the 9.1 L. Do two drain-and-fills rather than a pressure flush on an old box, and change the pan filter.

items.spec: EP90 / 80W-90 gear oil, API GL-4 or GL-5 · ≈2.3 L
items.interval: At purchase (Comma: change every 40,000 km / 24 months)
items.note: The filler at the back of the case is tapered, so it feels tight before it is fully seated. Don't overtighten it. Use a new copper washer on the drain plug. The intermediate shaft and rear output seals are the usual leaks.

parts.name: EP90 gear oil and LT230 drain/fill plugs
LT230 output flange oil seal FRC7043

items.spec: EP80W-90 GL-4/GL-5 · front ≈1.7 L. Rear ≈1.7 L on the Rover axle (one data set lists 2.3 L for the NAS D90). 110/130 (Salisbury) rear 2.26 L, 90 rear 1.7 L (Haynes)
items.interval: At purchase, then every 2 years (Comma: 40,000 km / 24 months)
items.note: Fill each axle to the level plug on level ground. The Tdi manual figure is 1.7 L, but one Defender2 owner got nearly 2 L into a rear axle on level ground, so trust the level plug rather than the book. Use a new drain-plug washer.

parts.name: Differential drain plug washers and EP90

items.spec: Early trucks: EP90 · 0.35 L per side (handbook). From about 1994: one-shot swivel grease STC3435, one sachet per side
items.interval: Check at purchase and every service. Comma says change every 40,000 km / 24 months
items.note: Lucky8 lists the STC3435 sachet for the NAS Defender 90 ('94–'97) and the Defender 110 ('93), but a 1997 NAS D90 data set still lists 0.35 L of EP oil, and JC's British 4x4's 52,500 km service checklist for the NAS 90 and 110 also calls for EP gear oil in the swivels, so check what is actually in yours before topping up [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]. An AULRO owner's 1994 swivel took about 450 ml to reach the level plug, so fill until it just dribbles out. Weeping seals mean the chrome ball is pitted. See the repairs above.

parts.name: Front axle swivel ball oil seal LR059968

items.spec: Dexron IID ATF (Haynes) · 2.8 L system. The 1993 US service checklist says ATF Type F instead, so check what's in yours before topping up. Steering box: EP80W-90
items.note: Leaks from the box's input seal or sector shaft are common. Top up and watch the level.

parts.name: Power steering box seals and hoses

items.interval: At purchase, then every 18 months (Comma: change every 30,000 km / 18 months)
items.note: The hydraulic clutch shares the fluid type. A soft clutch pedal usually means the slave cylinder is failing.

items.spec: Multipurpose lithium grease on the UJs and sliding joints
items.interval: At purchase. Comma says check UJs every 12 months and sliding joints every 24 months
items.note: A clunk on take-up usually means a dry UJ or a worn sliding spline. Grease them before chasing the gearbox.
